prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks

statement.case_for: I moved B030 from my eighth place to first after reading the ballots. Seven of eight members ranked it, four placed it in their top three, and the colleagues who know atomic structure best (Lindroth and Kroll) put it first. The reasons that matter to me are the ones I apply to any candidate. It is an original invention: Katori's 2001-2003 magic-wavelength proposal and his first lattice-clock demonstration. It is an instrument that opens a door, because clocks at the 1e-18 level let people measure relativistic redshift across millimetres, test constants and prepare for a redefinition of the second. It is also experimentally verified in a way few results are, since independent clocks in Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Germany and China agree with one another at that level. Most important for my own test of whether the people credited actually did the original work, the attribution is the cleanest on the shortlist: a proposer-and-first-demonstrator (Katori) and the experimenter who drove the accuracy and many-body regime (Ye). Nobody on the shortlist asks us to choose three from five or four, or to draw a line through a collaboration of hundreds. The citation can be written narrowly around the lattice clock so that it does not touch the 2005 frequency-comb prize or the 2012 ion-control prize.
statement.case_against: My original reservation stands in part. The value of the clock to humanity is mainly metrological and still prospective, because the redefinition of the second has not happened. A strict reading of 'discovery or invention' could also ask whether a record in precision is a discovery at all, and whether the lattice clock is sufficiently separate from Hall and Hansch's comb work and Wineland's ion work. Priority is not entirely closed either: Lemonde, Takamoto and others made early demonstrations, and the ion-clock community has parallel credit. Against my own earlier ranking, B017 is the better answer to 'a central question about nature', but its attribution is much weaker. I regard that as a reason to prefer B030 now, not as a reason to dismiss the Higgs experiments.

responses.point: Kroll ranked B030 first as a measurement instrument that changed what can be measured (geodesy, constants, dark-matter searches, a coming redefinition of the second), with Katori proposing and first demonstrating and Ye driving accuracy, and no conflict with the 2005 comb prize.
responses.response: I now agree with the substance and was too hard on it in my opening. The strongest point is your separation from the 2005 prize: the magic-wavelength idea is a different invention from the comb. I still qualify the 'changed what can be measured' claim. Geodesy and dark-matter searches are demonstrations and prospects, not yet routine uses, so I would put the citation on the invention and realization of the clock itself and leave the applications out of the wording.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked B030 first because magic-wavelength trapping is a genuinely new idea resting on atomic polarizability, with clocks well below the caesium standard, and noted that the share between proposal and Boulder realization could be argued.
responses.response: Your atomic-physics reading is what changed my mind, since I could not settle that priority question myself from the microscopy side. I accept the two-name configuration but I would like you to test the share question explicitly before the final ballot: please say whether Katori's 2001-2003 proposal and early Sr demonstration together carry the originality, or whether Ye's many-body and comb-linked work is of equal weight. If Lemonde's group has a real claim to the early demonstrations, we should know that before we claim it is clean.

responses.point: Pearce ranked B020 (IceCube) first as a landmark of detector-driven astroparticle physics that opened a new observational window, while asking for expert review of attribution among Halzen, Karle, Spiering, AMANDA and Baikal.
responses.response: I share your admiration for the instrument and ranked it third. My difficulty is exactly the attribution you flag: we would be crediting three people from a collaboration of hundreds, with the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND history in the background, and I want to be absolutely sure of who did the original work. The source picture (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068) is also still developing. I keep it as a strong alternative, and I would be willing to support it if expert reviewers can document that the three names are defensible.

responses.point: Danielsson ranked B055 (precision CMB mapping) first as the discovery that put numbers on the age, geometry and composition of the universe, with Bennett, Spergel and Puget spanning WMAP and Planck.
responses.response: The scientific importance is not in doubt, but I disagree on whether it fits this prize. COBE already received the original CMB anisotropy discovery, and WMAP and Planck are a later, more precise version of that measurement, which is what I mean by it not being the original experiment. The attribution problem you describe (WMAP against Planck, Page, and the instrument teams) is also severe. I did not rank it in my top eight, and I would need a convincing argument that a precision refinement is a new discovery.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked B058 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) first as a new class of matter, a clean theory-then-experiment story that builds on the 2016 topology prize without repeating it.
responses.response: This is a fine scientific case and I did not rank it, mainly for attribution reasons that your own ballot acknowledges. The HgTe prediction came from Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, and Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan did the three-dimensional work, so any trio omits people with strong claims. Zhang's death also removes a name that the historical record would normally include. I would also want to know how well the edge conduction in HgTe is quantized, since you note it is not perfect. I take it seriously but not as my preferred option.

uncertainties: Whether Lemonde's group or other early lattice-clock demonstrations have a priority claim that would complicate the two-name credit.
Whether the committee regards a metrology record as a discovery or invention in the statutory sense, given that the redefinition of the second has not yet occurred.
How to word the citation so that it is clearly distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize.
Whether the Higgs experiments (B017) could be given a defensible three-name credit from Gianotti, Jenni, Virdee, Della Negra and Evans; if so I would reconsider.
statement.conflict_note: I have been a Fellow of the University of Tokyo since 2025 and have long-running exchanges with the University of Tokyo, and Hidetoshi Katori is, to my knowledge, based there (also RIKEN). I have no collaboration or personal tie to him or to Jun Ye, but the committee should note this institutional connection in case it requires recusal on B030. My Chalmers colleague Goran Johansson is a committee member and not a candidate, and no other specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile.
